etymologies.etymologyHTML: 1580s; From mathematic (noun) +‎ -ics, from Middle English mathematique, methametik, matematik, matamatik, from Old French mathematique, from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “on the matter of that which is learned”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, study, learning”). Displaced native Old English rīmcræft.

definitions.definition: An abstract representational system studying numbers, shapes, structures, quantitative change and relationships between them.

quote.citation: 1992 March 2, Richard Preston, “The Mountains of Pi”, in The New Yorker:
quote.text: Looking at the Leibniz series, you feel the independence of mathematics from human culture. Surely, on any world that knows pi the Leibniz series will also be known... Nilakantha, an astronomer, grammarian, and mathematician who lived on the Kerala coast of India, described the formula in Sanskrit poetry around the year 1500.

quote.citation: 2002, Ian Stewart, Does God Play Dice?: The New Mathematics of Chaos, page 38:
quote.text: The answer is 'yes', and the mathematics needed is the theory of probability and its applied cousin, statistics.

definitions.definition: A person's ability to count, calculate, and use different systems of mathematics at differing levels.
